Slide Hampton

Trombonist and arranger Slide Hampton was born on April 21, 1932 in Jeannette, Pennsylvania. He has performed with Woody Herman, Maynard Ferguson and Dizzy Gillespie, and played a major role in Gillespie’s United Nations Orchestra. His arrangements have been performed by numerous ensembles including the Carnegie Hall Jazz Band and the Collective Black Artists’ Orchestra.
Slide was interviewed in West Orange, New Jersey on July 30, 2003 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe and we are in West Orange, New Jersey for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. I’m very pleased to have Slide Hampton with me today. And you know an interviewer is not supposed to tell stories, but I must tell you that a couple of years ago I heard your band at the Iridium.
Oh yes.

And I happened to get a seat that was right at the end of the saxophone section. And I was able actually to see the music. And I saw this passage coming up. I said this is totally impossible. They cannot play this. And not only did they play it but the whole band, in unison, played this lick that I was just astounded at.
“Night in Tunisia.”
Yes. I could not believe they pulled it off. You write some challenging music.
When we first played that and Paquito D’Rivera heard that he said, “God, what was that?”
It was a unison lick, right?
Yeah. I actually made it up — it was actually a sort of a copy from the Charlie Parker break that he had made.
Yeah. That was great. I just had to tell you that, that it certainly made an impression.

Well we just played that arrangement — not that arrangement, another arrangement of “Night in Tunisia” when I was in Holland a couple of weeks ago. And when I got ready to give them that break too but I didn’t have the courage to give it.
Really. So you do have some sympathy for where you are at and who is playing the music?

Oh yeah. You have to adjust you know. Because if you find a real enthusiastic bunch of guys then you give them any difficult music. And they’re glad to have the challenge. Other guys, “Oh man, this is difficult,” you know.
Well you have done both small group and big band music. Is there a place that you’re most comfortable in? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

You know you’re thinking — of course I’ve been asked that question many times and most musicians are. But see the thing is that we actually were raised in the big band period. And all the musicians that you hear playing the small groups that we aspired to, like Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie and Benny Goodman, Stan Getz, they all were raised in the big band period. And that was what prepared them so well to be so well presented in small groups, that big band experience. So actually we find both of them as important, but of course you can enjoy yourself in one way in a small group because you get to improvise more. And in the big band you have the wonderful experience of playing in the ensemble with other people, which is very important and wonderful also.
It might seem obvious to musicians what that positive experience of being in a big band is, but maybe for non-musicians who might see this tape, can you relate what kind of things you gain from that?

Well you know what people think when they see a person in a big group, they think that it is a kind of a situation that’s so well organized that it would kind of prevent you from being free enough to improvise. It’s not the case at all. Actually because improvisation is certainly a free style of playing music, but there is a lot of organization that goes on in an improvisation. To have a good improvisation there’s a composition that goes on, a certain amount of theory, a certain amount of all the things that you actually learned also in the large ensembles.
Hearing your note in place with everything else, I mean really helps your ear doesn’t it?

It does. And you hear the resolutions of the harmony, harmony of arrangements that are written by great arrangers. I remember when I played with the Dizzy Gillespie group and I was playing arrangements by Quincy Jones, by Dizzy himself, Ernie Wilkins, Melba Liston, Benny Golson. You learn about resolutions in the big group, because you hear all these resolving harmonies and things. So when you improvise you also use resolutions as a big part of the way that you make an improvisation.
That’s a great point. When you were growing up, did you have a musical family?

My mother and father, all my sisters and brothers were musicians. I was raised in Indianapolis which was a wonderful musical environment, because Freddie Hubbard was there, Wes Montgomery, J.J. Johnson, and just a lot of guys that were really very, very talented musicians that never became known. But we had a wonderful environment and the people there were very supportive of young people becoming musicians, in the high schools, marching band, they were very encouraging to us. So we were raised in an environment of music. In our family band we traveled throughout the country playing places.
Kind of — what were the venues? Were they dances or just parties and that kind of thing? © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

At one time all the venues that big bands, actually most of them were usually places that people were dancing. That was a big part of the inspiration for the music in general. Write something that will make the people dance. Because it’s a little backwards than the way it was in classical music. When you heard classical music you heard music that is actually coming from a dance. First it was a dance and then there was the music.
Like the gavotte. Those things.
Yeah. Yeah see?
That’s a great point.

And in jazz, first it was the music and then there was the dance you see. So that was a very inspiring part of it but we also finally played at Carnegie Hall, Apollo Theater, and again the Savoy Ballroom, where everybody is dancing again, like a thousand people are dancing, the floor is going up and down like this. And actually we played the Apollo, and then we went in the Savoy for two weeks, and we came, by popular demand, back in the Apollo again. And nobody ever did that. And the thing was that see in the Apollo you have these big shows. You have a lot of music. We didn’t read music. We had a couple of brothers that read but the rest of us didn’t read. They had to teach us the part. So we would learn the parts by memory and we played the show. And the people, they loved it.
That’s really neat. What year would this have been?
That was in the early — well I guess like in the early fifties.
Uh huh. And they could be — the Apollo could be, let’s say, unkind to people they didn’t like? Is that true?

They were kind of outspoken. If they didn’t like something they would say so. And actually it was a good point because it really did make people, when they went there, it made them do their very best. And some big stars actually from those talent shows came out of those talent shows. Because the competition was always so high. But if they liked you they would let you know it. And if they didn’t like you they would let you know.
I see. When did you first get the urge to become an arranger?

Well you know somebody was just asking me that question, and in the case of us, which are all the guys in Indianapolis, David Baker was there and of course J.J. Johnson, we all started to learn to arrange right with learning to play the instrument. Because we thought in order to be a complete musician you had to learn about theory, you had to learn about orchestration, you had to learn about arrangements, you had to learn about playing in the ensemble. So this was all a part of becoming a musician for us. And so the arranging everything came out along with learning to play the instruments.
I see. So it wasn’t really just like this separate decision, I can play now and then I need to be a writer too. Kind of just hand in hand? © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
In the case of many guys it was like that. But in our case, they fooled us right from the beginning and said you guys got to learn all of this right away. And we thought it was true, and we tried it.
And who was telling you this, your teachers?

The teachers. Oh yeah. They were teaching you theory and everything right from the beginning. In like in general, in the environment, you know we just had this great inspiration to try to learn how to arrange and to orchestrate. It was, a lot of it was a decision we made ourselves, we just wanted to know these things.
Sure. Who were the influences on the trombone for you back then?

There were many. At that time there were many trombone players that were very popular. Later in the fifties and sixties you started not to hear much of trombone players anymore. But in the forties and fifties there were a lot of trombone players that were popular. There was Tommy Dorsey, there was Trummy Young, there finally was J.J. Johnson, there was Jack Teagarden, there was Lawrence Brown. A thousand guys you know. So we were listening to all of them and actually we wasn’t really thinking about having a favorite. We were just loving all of it and learning, enjoying listening and learning from all of them.
Neat. You were, let’s see, you were born in ’32?
Yes.
And do you recall anything different about your family life during the World War II years?

Well all my brothers went in the Army. And of course they were all in bands in the Army. You know that was very lucky for them. But they saw also some of the war action too, some of them did, and they told me about how it was and everything. But they did a lot of studying, being in the Army bands, and got to actually rub elbows with a lot of great musicians and they learned a lot being there, and they came back even more developed in the areas of reading music, playing in the ensembles and writing music and all of that.
Were they overseas?
Yes.
You know we’re so used to almost instant communication nowadays. We almost forget about that it must have been tough on your parents to like wait for letters from the sons.
For some reason we never had a thought of any of them getting hurt in the Army.
Really.

We did have one brother that got hurt but I mean he had to go in the hospital, but we never thought of losing anybody. We never thought like that. Our family was so — my mother and father were such wonderful people. What I remember about my whole childhood is just being in a very wonderful environment of people that had a wonderful © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

way of relating to each other. They taught me just a wonderful thing about attitude and all of that. And our attitude was that we knew they were gonna come back. No matter what happened, we knew they were coming back. And they did.
Was the church part of your upbringing?
Oh yeah. My mother used to make me go to church every Sunday. I couldn’t get away from Indianapolis soon enough so I didn’t have to do that anymore. She had me in church all day.
Oh. All day. Was it a musical church?

It always had some music but it wasn’t like some of the churches that you go — like in Philadelphia there are some churches that got some choirs, and some of them actually have musical bands and things there. It was all singing and all but in our house there was music every day.
I see.

We were practicing and rehearsing every day. And all the people from the neighborhood were coming around. And the kids would come, and some of them would come in and learn about being musicians. My father was teaching everybody. He was a fantastic man.
Oh. And did he have work besides music too? During the day?

He did. My father could do everything. He was a great painter. He painted beautiful pictures. He was a carpenter. He was a school teacher. He did everything. That’s when you had that big family, he was actually very idealistic. Most people wouldn’t try to raise a family man, he had about ten kids you know. Most people wouldn’t try that. He didn’t think that was anything. He really felt as though he could handle that with no problem, because he could do so many things. And he did. He took care of us from the time that we were — until we were ready to leave home with no problem.
That’s wonderful. Do you have photos from back then?

I was just looking at my father and mother’s photos before I came here today, and a picture of our family band, one when I was very young and I wasn’t playing, I was dancing and singing in the band, and then one when I was older playing trombone.
That’s so interesting. Did you have people for a rhythm section, the whole—
Oh yeah. We had the rhythm section and everything right there in the family.
That’s neat. I sometimes wonder in those kind of situations your parents are thinking well let’s see, we need a saxophone player so—
I think that’s the way it was. They finally needed a trombone. I was the last one born into the family.
Oh, you were the youngest.
So they said we need a trombone player. You’re going to play trombone. And your name will be Slide whether you like it or not. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
Does that go back that far?
Yeah.
Your nickname?
Yes. From the time I started. I started actually playing trombone at 12. And when they gave me the trombone they gave me the name.
Is that right?
Yeah.
Because, is your name Locksley Wellington?
Yes.
Yeah I got that out of the Grove Dictionary.
Yeah. Not many people know that.
Yeah. Okay. That’s really interesting, that they pinned that on you right away. Well nicknames help too.
Oh yeah.
That’s great. Did you feel a need at a certain age to, you mentioned getting out of Indianapolis. Time to spread your own wings a little bit?

Well see when we played the Apollo Theater we had such success that the booking agents wanted us to stay in New York. And we would have had a good success in New York. But my sisters wanted to go back to Indianapolis. You know how ladies are. And so we didn’t stay. And after I was in New York the first time I remember when I was there I went to Birdland to hear Bud Powell play. That was it for me. I had to come to New York after that. And that’s all I talked about from that time until I got to New York is I have to go to New York. And I just had this great feeling for New York. And all I could think about was how can I get to New York. So I finally left Indianapolis on my way to New York, fifteen dollars in my pocket. So I only got as far as Cincinnati, Ohio. But I played with Miles there. Played with Miles for a weekend. And then some friends found out that I was in Cincinnati. They were in Houston, Texas. They sent for me to come from Cincinnati to Houston. So I took a bus ride from Cincinnati to Houston, Texas. It was horrible. Long and painful and hot. And I stayed in Houston for a year playing, because they had a great job there. They played one night a week in a club and it was a big success. I played with that band until Buddy Johnson heard me. And then he came and took me to New York City.
So you took the long way. Did you have your first arrangement played with him? With Buddy Johnson?
Well actually — probably the first professional arrangement, yes.
Yeah. Do you have the ability to sit at a desk like this and write?
I used to. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
I mean do you need to be near a piano?

I used to write without the piano. I wrote a lot of the arrangements, after I wrote for Buddy Johnson I wrote for Lionel Hampton and I wrote for Maynard. And a lot of the arrangements I wrote for Maynard I wrote without the piano. And those are recorded things. I was a young guy, you know, I had the energy that it takes to actually do that.
Well speaking of that, I have to play something for you. Because it’s something I really think is —
[audio interlude]
Do you remember this?
You know I’d forgotten about this song.
No kidding.
“Mark of Jazz.”
“Mark of Jazz.” Yeah. You were writing hot licks way back then too.

Yeah. Maynard gave us a lot of opportunity to arrange and to learn about arranging. So we were inspired writing there in that band. So there were several guys that were writing a lot. Willie Maiden and Don Sebesky and a couple of other guys that were in the band. Then we were playing arrangements by great arrangers from other bands too.
That was a hot group.
Yeah it was. People really liked that band. We certainly did.
This was ‘57ish.
Yes.
Did the group like that, being integrated, run into any problems?
Not really. Not really.
Glad to hear that.

I think the only time that we had any problems like that was when we took a whole tour. It was Sonny Rollins and his quartet, or no it was the trio, and it was Dave Brubeck with his group, Maynard Ferguson’s band. And then there was another, might have been The Four Freshmen or somebody like that. And we played really all through the south you know, because it was such a big thing that they would command everywhere for it. And we had some problems about finding places to eat and things like that once in a while. The whole thing wasn’t like that, but once in a while it was. But when I was with Buddy Johnson’s band, we couldn’t eat at any of those places. We couldn’t go in any hotels or anything like that.
In what parts of the country?

Well as soon as you get down below Washington I guess, down to Virginia, then it was all very difficult. But we were so much into the music, we weren’t thinking about that you know. That’s the wonderful thing about a lot of the guys that came before us, that © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

had more of those problems than we did. The music was so important to them that they just rode right through all of that. Music is like that. It’s really wonderful. It’s above everything. It’s above wars, it’s above racism, it’s above everything. Because see in the war, the guys that were having the jam sessions in the basement in Germany, the Germans, if they had been caught they would have been killed. They were still having jam sessions, playing Charlie Parker or Duke Ellington in the basement with the windows covered with stuff so nobody would know. They took that kind of chance. That’s how important the music was to them.
That’s right, ‘cause that regime felt that jazz music was evil.

Oh yeah. And there’s a lot of music that they didn’t allow the people to listen to or play. But jazz was so important to the guys that they had to play it anyhow. I played with a lot of those guys when I lived in Europe.
Yeah you spent a number of years, almost nine years or so, in Europe. Was that a planned decision or did you go there and like it on trip or something?

It was spontaneous. It wasn’t planned. Impromptu. I was playing with Woody Herman. And at that time when you joined a band you didn’t have any rehearsals or anything like that. You joined the band and you went right on the concert stage and played right there and you had to sight read everything and all of that. But we were always into that. Sight reading and all of that was a part of what we did for fun. When I was with Woody we played England for two weeks. And I have a very funny story with Woody because I was new in the band so his conducting I wasn’t familiar with. You know? So I’m just trying to follow the conductor. Because I feel when you give a downbeat I’m playing. But I was playing alone when he gave it out. So every time he would give a downbeat I would play, bamm. And then the band would play after me. So I’m wondering what’s going on, you know I said am I not seeing this right or what? So after the first week he came to me and said, “Slide, I’m paying you more money than anybody in the band. You’re the only one that’s playing wrong.” I said, “I know it. I just can’t figure out where your downbeat is.” And I says, “Is it here, is it here?” And the guys told me later they said, “We don’t play on his downbeat. He gives the downbeat and then we play when we think we should play.” So I said I’d wait for them. And after I played with him for two weeks some people found out that I was in England. They said while you’re over there come over on the continent of Europe and play some concerts over here. And I had never done this. And I didn’t know the condition. I didn’t know what the conditions would be. But they offered me such wonderful conditions. First class transportation, first class hotel, great money for the group and the concerts and everything. So I went over and played a few concerts and it was so unusual for me to be treated like that. I stayed for eight years.
Wow. And playing mostly with European musicians? © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Sometimes with American musicians, sometime with European musicians. I played with Dexter Gordon, Johnny Griffin, Benny Bailey, oh just a host of guys that were living — Kenny Clarke. All the guys that were living over there and also with the European musicians. We made radio shows. Because see in every city in Europe there’s a radio band that is subsidized by the government to play a certain amount of jazz every year.
Isn’t that something.

That money — they can only use that money for jazz projects. And they have that same subsidy for classical music and for folk music. So we had a lot of radio shows and television shows and cultural houses where we were playing concerts and festivals and all that. So it was really a fantastic experience.
And you were treated pretty darn well then.
Treated really — I never had that kind of treatment before. It was a surprise to me.
What prompted you to come back?
Well after I stayed over there for a while then I was asked to come back to do this CD with Dexter Gordon. The “Sophisticated Giant” CD.
Oh yeah. That’s a good one.

And for us it was a wonderful project. And I had worked with Dexter over there several times. He was just wonderful to work with. I had known of him before but I didn’t know him before and I had no idea what kind of person he was or anything. But working with him was like heaven. He treated everybody — musicians and audience alike — with all the love in the world you know. So I learned a lot working with him from that. And when he asked me to come back and do that, and asked me to stay. And I came back and things were starting to change in America then. People were becoming interested in jazz again.
Wasn’t there a song on that record called “Fried Bananas?” Something like that?
Yes. That’s Dexter’s original tune.
Those are marvelous arrangements and it’s such a nice sized ensemble, with the vibes in there, right?
Yeah.
Just — the colors are great on it.
I could have done a much better job with the arranging.
You think so?
Yeah. I was shooting the stuff off and then not really getting it. I was shooting.
Yeah. Well you’re probably your own worst critic when it comes to something like that.

Well you always — because you know when you have a chance to do something like that you really want to do something that has some real meaning and some real value. Because to get all of those guys together, because some of them were still living in © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
Europe and they were coming from all over the place and they had wonderful attitudes. They worked together very professional and very loving.
And you would get not a lot of studio time, right? To pull something like that off?

No you never get much studio time. In fact one of the CDs that we’ve done recently, we produced it ourselves, it’s the first time that we’ve had enough time in the studio to really do it the way that we should. Because then it was always you were running through those things and you know they were trying to be as considerate as possible. But it can only go on so long then they’d say, “Listen, you’ve got to move on.”
Yeah. You have mentioned coming back and that the country seemed to be taking a little more interest in jazz music. That’s interesting that you say that, because this was late seventies?
Yeah.
Was it the start of the educational interest in the music?

Yes it was. That was one of the things that opened up to the jazz musicians. We were offered — I’ve been offered many jobs in universities. But I never went to high school so I couldn’t take them. I’d have to tell the truth and say I’m not really — I don’t have the credentials for this. You know I had the experience for it and things like that but I don’t have the credentials and I’m not going to lie about a thing like that. But I would always, when I was offered a job like that I would recommend somebody that did have the credentials that also had the ability.
Yeah. You know there’s a lot of people who have the credentials though who don’t have the experience so, I mean you have the real life, hands on experience, and that’s worth a great deal.

Experience is very important of course, and the thing that’s most important of all is to be true to yourself. To tell the truth to yourself and to everyone else, that’s very important. Because that’s what improvisation actually is about. It’s about saying what the truth is about your feelings and about your experience, and about what it is that you can do and what you can’t do. The thing that improvisation does for me, it makes me realize that I don’t have to feel bad about the things that I can’t do, but I have to admit it. Because then it’s an advantage to me. If I try to make myself believe that I can do things that I can’t do, I’m being a disadvantage to myself. And improvisation is like that. It makes you admit the truth about yourself. The good and the bad. There’s plenty of bad.
That’s a great thought. I really like the way you put that. I can envision getting in a position where you are expected to play in a certain style and it just wouldn’t be you.
Yeah.
And trying to do it and it wouldn’t last too long I would guess. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
I’m not good at playing in different styles. Unless it’s something that I just feel to do because of the situation I’m in, I’m not good at being able to reproduce what other guys have done.
If you were to describe the style you like to play in or your own trombone style, is it possible to put it into words?

Yes, very easily. Because see the trombone, that instrument actually was — we kind of gave a false impression in many cases, because they would think about the circus. You know you hear the trombone [scats]. But the trombone actually was invented to play melodies. That’s what it was invented for. And that’s where it’s the most beautiful is when it’s playing melody. Because that’s the strong point that I work on in my own development is the ability to play melodies and to make lines that I play of other improvisations sound melodious. Because there’s one thing that I found out about people. They can relate to a melody. And especially one that they’ve already heard, but even if they haven’t heard it and it’s beautiful, they can relate to it. And once you’ve played one song that they know, everything you play after that they’ll try their best to understand it. So that’s my style, is trying to be melodious, and try to develop — I work on my sound. I want to have the most beautiful sound that I can. So when somebody hears it, even before they think about what I’m playing they say that sounds good. That feels good. That sounds good.
Great thoughts again. You have like these things you’re saying that ought to be put in stone somewhere.
Thank you.
What to you makes a good melody?

Well like anything else, the construction of a melody. The way that it resolves naturally from one note to the other. And of courses you know you have a lot of practice in that all of the great people that came before you that wrote melodies. There’s so many great melodies that started I don’t know how long ago, a thousand years ago even maybe. But to have a melody that a person can listen to. I thought about that recently — a melody that a person can listen to that they never heard before but they still can appreciate it and enjoy it. The beauty of it. Of course you can always enjoy a melody that you know, if it’s something that you like. But to be able to play a melody or to write a melody or compose a melody that people can listen to and say yeah I like that, although I haven’t heard it before. I think that’s one of the things that — the standards that I try to look for in playing or writing a melody.
If I was to arrange for a commission for you and leave it totally wide open, maybe describe the instrumentation or something, but at any rate just say we want a Slide © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
Hampton composition but we want a new thing. Where do you start with something like that?

Well I’ve been asked the question many times how do you start to approach either a composition or an arrangement. You have to start actually just be getting an idea of what it is that whoever you’re going to do it for, wants. And then to let it develop in a natural way. And the feeling for it, and the idea of it in your mind, let it develop in a natural way. So if you say you want a composition and you have a certain instrumentation, that instrumentation alone can inspire you a place to start. Once you get a place to start then the rest of it is natural development after that. I’ve had situations where I’ve been commissioned to do things for the Joe Henderson big band CD and when they gave me the composition, the first thing I try to do is find a melody. If you find a good melody — see because a good melody stands by itself. That’s an arrangement, that’s the composition, that’s everything, the theory and everything. If you find a good melody then the rest of the things are going to fall into place see. So if you’re going to arrange something for instance, you find a song that inspires you to arrange. And actually I feel like, except for people that write just to make a living, the only way that a person should approach an arrangement is by inspiration. So that whatever they’re inspired to do will leave some kind of long lasting musical standard that inspires the next person to write something that’s valuable. So I would start probably with finding a melody. And from that melody I would find the introduction later, the interludes, the way it’s going to resolve into other melodies, the way that it’s finally going to develop.
Does the individual you’re writing for shape the way you write also?

Well it can, you know if you have people that you really are familiar with and love the way they play. But you still have to write — I like to write something that anybody can play it and enjoy it. The enjoyment of the musician is one of the very first things to me, that they enjoy playing it. Because I know that if they enjoy playing it they’re going to get a certain feeling across to the people that are listening to it. That inspiration is going to make everything. Because see music is not — when you write music down, that’s not music. Music is what somebody interprets from that thing that you write down. And that’s when the music starts is when the musicians get it and decide what they’re going to do with it and start to develop it. See whenever you heard some of the recordings and things that we liked of the big bands, Glenn Miller, Duke Ellington, Count Basie, they had played that music for a long time before they recorded it see. They didn’t go in the studio like we do now, they give you a whole bunch of new music and you go in there and learn it and record it. I mean it’s still new to you. There’s so much that you could do if you really get to know it. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

That’s true. Those songs that they recorded back then had been tweaked and just gotten to that wonderful point where they were ready to record. Wow. Do you — this is kind of a technical question — do you write a transposed score when you work?
A transposed score. I could easily write a concert score, but you know what I think about? I think about the poor guy that has to transpose it. You know?
That’s nice of you.

Let him do all of that transposition, you know. I think man, boy that must be a job. So I always did develop the transposed score approach. And I also write with a pen or pencil. I don’t use computers or anything like that. I enjoy writing the traditional way.
Yeah. Well it also helps I guess if you’re writing a transposed score is you actually know what you’re asking these people to pull off — from a saxophone standpoint and that whole thing.
That’s true, the range. Because when you write a concert score you still have to keep in mind the range of the instruments and everything.
If you look at a piece that you’re writing and you look down beat one of a particular measure that you’ve written, how much of that can you hear in your head?

Well what I do, I’m writing a score right now and it’s for two flutes, clarinet, bass clarinet, nine violins, three violas, two cellos, bass, three trombones, three trumpets, piano, bass, drums, guitar, percussion. And what I do is I think everything starts off, usually to me, I mean in life, things usually don’t hit you right over the head. They usually start off as something, maybe as a smaller approach to a conversation or whatever, rather than just coming in and really throwing a lot of words at you. You know, so I start off with the thing being not too — I don’t like to start off with everything at once. I like for it to start small and develop. Because I think it does a lot of good for the human ear and for the people that are going to listen when they have a chance, if you give them a chance to get used to it before you throw the whole thing at them. Some people like to throw the whole thing right in the beginning. When I’m playing it’s the same way. I like to start my concerts not too fast, not too loud, not too big. Just give the people a chance to let their ears get used to the music. And then as they do then you can given them some more dissonant things, some more volume and stuff like that, in and out of those things. So I like to let a thing develop from a small beginning, in and out, and use more of the instruments, not use them all through the whole thing, change and like that.

In the ensemble?
Yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

Well it’s not really a problem because actually when you’re looking at the score you always are inspired to use, probably more often than not, things that don’t have to be there. The whole idea I find is the simplicity is where you get the most value out of the thing. When you can write simple. That means that when you do write complicated or write the whole ensemble it has more of a purpose. But you can always use, especially if you have good musicians. That’s the thing that affects it. The level of musicianship that you’re dealing with. You can write one person playing when it’s a really good musician, and it will have a good effect. But if it’s a musician that doesn’t have very much experience and you write them by theirselves it can feel uncertain. But you know all the instruments can always be used in so many ways to make the different colors, the different effects, and to make as much variety as possible. That’s very important.

So I didn’t contribute that much to him until later when I joined the United Nations band. I started doing some writing for that. But it was always still very intimidating to be writing for him, because he was such a great arranger himself. Standards were very high.
Yeah. Is there certain things that he liked to hear? Is it possible to answer that? I mean certain tempos, feels? I know he loved Latin grooves.

Well he liked Latin things but he didn’t mind it not being Latin. The thing that he looked for was the sincerity of the essence of the arrangement or composition. They were very — all of their arrangements had a real strong expressive aspect. So they wrote things that you had to work on. If you weren’t a virtuoso you still had to do a lot of practice to try to play whatever it is that they wrote. So the music was based on that kind of thing, you know, it was a very sincere music and the music had a lot of feeling and a lot of expression, and was very inspiring to all the music world in general. You go back and see this guy that came from a place in the south where he was living in a situation where racism and all of that was really rampant. Yeah. To get to hear those things, and experiment, and find out what works and what doesn’t.

We did a lot of that in Europe already before I came back you know. In fact in Europe they had some subsidy for projects that were based on free music, that means that you were usually doing things that were somewhat unusual to the way that you usually approach composing or writing music. And I thought it was a thing that had a good effect on, in general, on our musical growth, because it was a chance for us to experience something different in music. And it was a chance to do something that ordinarily would — well it gave us a chance to be completely free. Okay what happens when you’re completely free, and see what happens. The only thing that I didn’t agree with about it is when you have a musical concept that’s new, I think you should always still have a relationship to the music that comes before so that you can see where that relates to the music. Don’t always — you shouldn’t always jump off and do something that you can’t tell if it has anything to do with all the stuff that came before, because all the music that came before is the reason that something should happen. Sometimes people make it happen because they didn’t want to have a contact with the thing that happened before, and things don’t happen like that. Things develop from one stage, and they don’t all of a sudden, the glacier didn’t all of a sudden jump from North America then jump to South America. It would have been a mess if it had. So music is the same way. You can’t disconnect it.
I see.

You can be as advanced as you want, but don’t disconnect it. Still keep the development process in a natural process from the traditional thing, come all the way up and go as far as you want to, but somehow be able to go back and see how that line connects. Because that’s the way nature is. And no matter how much we want to do a thing we still have to go by the rules of nature.
Yeah. That’s very interesting again. And you’ve also done some work in I guess you could call it the popular music field with some Motown artists and that kind of thing?
Yeah.

What’s your feeling about jazz today?

Well I’ve been asked that question recently and see the wonderful thing about jazz is where jazz comes from and why is the thing that answers when people think is jazz going to live, is it going to die? Jazz is one of the only art forms where people have the freedom of expression. And you don’t have to say anything bad about anybody to do what you © Fillius Jazz Archive -22-

feel. You don’t have to do anything that actually rubs anybody the wrong way to do what you feel. There’s no language where you’re saying anything that offends — you don’t offend anybody. You don’t make anybody think that personally you’re attacking them. It’s the only thing that you can do that with. You can express your exact feelings, and somehow people from everywhere have experienced those same things that you’re feeling. Jazz is one of the only things like that. So jazz is a music that comes from a very natural part of the human race in general. The thing that’s different about it is that it doesn’t allow any person or group to control it. That’s one of the most dangerous things about it. It makes people free. And all the big countries that are like the countries that have strong political parties and all of that, that’s frightening to them. Because the one thing they don’t want is for a person to have their own opinion about things. Jazz gives you the chance to have your own opinion. And that’s one of the really fantastic things about it. Even more than the music is that it gives you the chance to express how you’re feeling and also say yeah, well he had the right to say what he feels too. You have the right to play the way that he plays just as much as I do. And that’s what makes it wonderful is that all these different rights give you all these different possibilities and inspirations and all of that. So jazz will always exist. Because people have to, unless they finally just put everybody in the thing and just make them do whatever they want them to do forever, and even then there’ll be somebody slipping around trying to play a blues chorus.
